doc.title: Tyner McCoy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The West Philly neighborhood at May and Fairmount
summary: Tyner describes the corner where he grew up, its working-class mixed population and where he wrote 'Blues on the Corner'.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well let’s go back and let’s talk about the house that you lived in when you were coming up. Did you stay in the same house, did you stay in the same neighborhood? If you could identify where that neighborhood was in Philadelphia?
I was there quite a long time actually, and then later on I met John Coltrane and met my wife Aisha Tyner and life just sort of grew.
And in what part of town in Philadelphia was your-
West Philly.
West Philly. Do you remember the address or any of the street names in that neighborhood?
May street . . . May and Fairmount.
(Break in the recording)
So let’s pick it back up. We were talking about your neighborhood when you were growing up. We had identified Main St. and some of the other streets-
May street, (spells) M-a-y.
M-a-y.
May and Fairmount. Fairmount was a big street, May was a side street, but we were right on the corner. That’s where I wrote, “Blues on the Corner.” (laughs)
So what was that neighborhood like? Was it segregated, was it integrated, was it middle class, working class?
Sort of middle class, would you say, Honey?
Working class.
Working class, yeah.
And was it integrated or segregated at that time?
Uh, at that time, I think it was, I would say there was other people living there . . .
Different types.
Different types of people, yeah. Americans from different groups, white American, black Americans of different-
So it was an integrated neighborhood?
Yeah, kind of anyway, but mostly black.
Just on the forward edge of gentrification, because I know parts of Philadelphia were staunchly segregated through many periods of time.

Yeah, that’s true. Right, exactly. Because it was once a connected capitol kind of a thing. When the people landed on the ships that brought them from Europe, they would come up from Maryland, different places and then before you know it, they’re building a kind of uh . . . the east coast was full of immigrants, so there were a lot of descendants from those people.
